sources.cite: Microsoft Learn training, 'Explore Write Accelerator' (module Explore Azure storage for SAP workloads)
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-17. Relevant text: Write Accelerator is a disk capability for M-Series VMs with Premium managed disks that improves write latency, for the volumes that hold the DBMS transaction log; it 'isn't recommended for data volumes'; disk caching must be None or Read Only; only I/Os of 512 KiB or smaller are accelerated; per-VM limits, M64s: 8 Write Accelerator disks and 10,000 Write Accelerator IOPS shared by all of them. The 'Enable Write Accelerator' page (read 2026-11-18) shows az vm update --write-accelerator <lun>=true for an existing disk, limits it to M-series VMs on Premium SSD, and says to use it for transaction or redo log volumes, not data volumes. HANA's sub-millisecond log write expectation is SAP's guidance, not on that page (to verify against the SAP HANA storage page).

brief.situation: You are the Azure engineer for Pell & Hart's SAP landscape, migrated to Azure last weekend. Production HANA runs on hana-prd-1 (M64s) with /hana/log on two striped Premium SSD disks. Since this morning, finance reports postings taking seconds instead of milliseconds. Month-end closing jobs start at 18:00.
handover: The VMs were built from the wave-3 Bicep template; the template's disk section was copied from the application server template.
HANA's own alert: 'log write wait time high' since 08:40.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows the HANA VM, its log and data disks, their caching and Write Accelerator settings.
Each command takes a minute or two; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

hana.why: Wait for the running command to finish.

tmpl.label: grep the Bicep template's disk section
tmpl.why: Wait for the running command to finish.

effects.output:
basis@cloudshell:~$ grep -n -A3 'hana-log' bicep/wave3-hana.bicep | head -4
41:  name: 'hana-log-${{i}}'

effects.finding: The template set the wrong caching and left Write Accelerator off.

enable.label: In a 10-minute HANA stop agreed with finance: set the two log disks to caching None and enable Write Accelerator on them
enable.available: not busy and (not fixed and not harmed)
enable.why: Already done, or the system is down.

effects.output:
basis@cloudshell:~$ sapcontrol -nr 00 -function StopSystem HDB
basis@cloudshell:~$ az vm update -g rg-sap-prd -n hana-prd-1 --set storageProfile.dataDisks[4].caching=None storageProfile.dataDisks[5].caching=None --write-accelerator 4=true 5=true
provisioningState: Succeeded
basis@cloudshell:~$ sapcontrol -nr 00 -function StartSystem HDB

effects.log: The log disks now take the accelerated write path (it requires caching None or ReadOnly), and only the log volume uses it, which is what the feature is for.

template.label: Fix the Bicep template for the log disks and run a disk-settings check after every deployment
template.available: not busy and (not planned and not harmed)
template.why: Already done, or the system is down.

effects.output:
basis@cloudshell:~$ git diff bicep/wave3-hana.bicep
-  caching: 'ReadWrite'
-  writeAcceleratorEnabled: false
+  caching: 'None'
+  writeAcceleratorEnabled: true
basis@cloudshell:~$ echo './check-hana-disks --role log --expect caching=None,wa=true' >> pipelines/post-deploy.sh

effects.log: The next HANA VM is built right, and a post-deployment check catches a wrong log disk before HANA goes live.

allwa.label: Enable Write Accelerator on all six disks, data and log

effects.output:
basis@cloudshell:~$ az vm update -g rg-sap-prd -n hana-prd-1 --write-accelerator 0=true 1=true 2=true 3=true 4=true 5=true
provisioningState: Succeeded

effects.log: Write Accelerator is for log volumes, and its IOPS limit is shared by every accelerated disk: the data disks' writes now compete with the log for it, and the savepoints slow the commits.

parts.label: Why
parts.criteria: Connects log latency to disk settings.
parts.modelAnswer: HANA's log writes averaged 9.6 ms and iostat agreed. The log disks had ReadWrite caching and Write Accelerator off, copied from the application server template; a commit waits for its log write.

parts.label: Change
parts.criteria: Uses the feature where it belongs.
parts.modelAnswer: In an agreed short stop, set the two log disks to caching None and enabled Write Accelerator on them only; the feature needs caching None or ReadOnly, and it is meant for log volumes, its IOPS limit shared per VM.

parts.label: Next VM
parts.modelAnswer: The Bicep template now sets the log disks correctly, and a post-deployment check verifies them.

sharedLimit.headline: An accelerator for the log only
sharedLimit.body: Write Accelerator is for the transaction log, and its IOPS limit is per VM. Put it on the log disks only, with caching None.

closeSlow.headline: Every commit waits for the log
closeSlow.body: On M-series, HANA's log volume needs Write Accelerator and caching None. The template's copied settings were the cause.

accelerated.headline: Good: the log volume, configured as designed
accelerated.body: You compared the disk settings with HANA's log write time, changed only the log disks in an agreed window, checked the latency, and fixed the template that caused it.

scoring.modelReasoning: Commits wait for log writes, and HANA and iostat both show about 10 ms on the log stripe. The log disks have ReadWrite caching and no Write Accelerator because the template was copied from an application server. On M-series, the log volume should use Write Accelerator with caching None; change only the log disks in an agreed window, check the latency, and fix the template. Accelerating the data disks too shares the per-VM limit with the log; the network is not involved.
